questions.q: In which month and year was the Quit India Movement launched, and what was the immediate trigger that led Gandhi to give the "Do or Die" call?
questions.a: The Quit India Movement was launched in August 1942 after the failure of the Cripps Mission (March-April 1942), which offered only dominion status after the war — not immediate independence. A wrong answer (e.g., "1930" or "after Jallianwala Bagh") reveals the student is confusing this with the Civil Disobedience Movement or earlier events, missing the specific WWII context that made 1942 unique.

questions.q: Why did the British arrest the entire Congress leadership (Gandhi, Nehru, Patel, Azad) within 24 hours of the Quit India resolution, unlike in 1920 or 1930 when leaders led movements for months?
questions.a: The British feared the "Do or Die" call would trigger uncontrolled mass violence during WWII when they needed Indian troops and resources; they also saw the Congress as collaborating with the Japanese threat. A wrong answer (e.g., "British were always repressive") misses the strategic calculation: in 1920 and 1930, the British tolerated limited non-violence, but in 1942 wartime conditions made ANY mass uprising an existential threat to their war effort.

questions.q: A student reads a 1942 British intelligence report stating: "The movement has no central direction; local leaders act independently." How does this explain why the Quit India Movement saw parallel governments in Ballia, Satara, and Tamluk, unlike earlier movements?
questions.a: With top leaders jailed, local activists (students, socialists like Jayaprakash Narayan, peasants) took initiative, creating parallel administrations (prati sarkars) that collected taxes, ran courts, and maintained order — showing the movement had become a genuine mass uprising beyond Congress control. A wrong answer (e.g., "Congress planned this") reveals the student doesn't grasp how leaderlessness enabled radical local experimentation impossible in centrally directed movements.

questions.q: Compare the British response to the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) and the Quit India Movement (1942). What does the difference in repression (e.g., 1942: 10,000+ deaths, machine-gunning crowds, aerial bombing) reveal about British priorities in 1942?
questions.a: In 1920-22, the British used legal repression (arrests, bans) because the empire was stable; in 1942, they used military force (57 battalions, air power) because the movement coincided with the Japanese advance to India's borders — making it a wartime security crisis. A wrong answer (e.g., "British were always brutal") fails to analyze how WWII transformed a political challenge into a military emergency, explaining the unprecedented violence.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "The Quit India Movement failed because it was crushed within months and Congress leaders spent the rest of the war in jail." Defend your position with three pieces of evidence.
questions.a: The claim is incorrect. Evidence: (1) The movement proved British rule depended entirely on force, not consent — even Churchill admitted "Quit India" made post-war retention impossible. (2) Parallel governments demonstrated Indians could self-govern. (3) The 1945-46 INA trials and naval mutiny showed the movement's spirit survived in the armed forces. A wrong answer treating "suppression = failure" misses how movements can succeed politically even when militarily defeated — a key historical reasoning skill.

questions.q: Create a 4-panel storyboard showing how a 16-year-old student in 1942 Bombay decides to join the Quit India Movement despite her father's opposition. Each panel must show a different historical factor influencing her decision (wartime hardship, Cripps failure, "Do or Die" speech, peer pressure).
questions.a: A strong answer shows: Panel 1 — Family struggling with wartime inflation/rationing (economic cause). Panel 2 — Newspaper headline "Cripps Mission Fails: No Independence Till War Ends" (political trigger). Panel 3 — Hearing Gandhi's "Do or Die" radio broadcast at August Kranti Maidan (emotional catalyst). Panel 4 — Friends from college socialist group distributing cyclostyled pamphlets urging student strike (peer network). A weak answer uses generic "patriotism" without specific 1942 factors, showing inability to contextualize individual agency in historical conditions.
